correctness.rationale: The claim is finite and exactly specified. The verifier reconstructs all \(256\) words and \(64\) deletion outputs, models one-deletion correction by the exact pairwise-disjoint-shadow set-packing constraints, independently re-establishes the optimum cardinality \(24\), obtains coverage minimum \(60\) and maximum \(64\), proves infeasibility of coverages \(61\) and \(63\), and tests every integer shadow-size profile in that interval. Exactly the six stated profiles are feasible. Every surviving profile has an explicit 24-word witness whose deletion shadows are checked directly without trusting the optimizer incumbent. The historical Table 2 code is separately reconstructed and has profile \( (4,12,0,8) \). The main residual correctness risk is reliance on the mixed-integer solver for finite infeasibility certificates; this is disclosed and no infinite conclusion is drawn.

broader_coverage.reasoning: The even-alphabet theorem is broader in alphabet size for cardinality and existence, but it supplies constructions rather than a classification of every optimal code by descendant-set profile. Existence of one nonperfect and one perfect optimum does not rule out intermediate defects or determine which of the combinatorially possible profiles occur.

value.rationale: The quaternary case is the smallest nonbinary even alphabet in the classical sharp length-four theorem, and the primary paper itself juxtaposes an explicit nonperfect optimum with a later perfect construction. Classifying all possible deletion-shadow profiles answers the natural structural question left between those two endpoints: maximum cardinality permits only defects \(4\), \(2\), or \(0\), with six exact profiles. This is a complete equality invariant for a canonical finite benchmark, not an arbitrary parameter slice or a recomputation of the known optimum.
